description: We are a team of SAR explorers - passionate about space exploration, technology and understanding our planet through science and innovation. Our goal is to explore how NASA's Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology can reveal changes on Earth's surface and turn observation into meaningful solutions for real world challenges.
summary:
SAR Explorer is a web prototype for comparing two prepared NASA–ISRO NISAR radar images over Rasuwa, Nepal. Users upload matching GeoTIFFs to view the before-and-after observations, a color-coded radar-return difference, and the area that crosses a selected decrease threshold.

The project makes satellite radar comparisons more approachable and helps highlight places that may merit further investigation. It is important because remote areas can be difficult to survey, and satellite data can support timely follow-up with local reports and field observations. The results are only a screening signal: radar changes do not confirm flooding, damage, or when an event occurred, so the app is not an official map or warning system.

This project can be a foundation for future enhancement incorporating AI to detect Surface movement and notify accordingly.
details:
Project: SAR Explorer — NISAR Change Viewer

What it does and how it works
SAR Explorer is a web application for comparing two radar observations of the same area. Its initial study area is Rasuwa, Nepal, in the context of the August 2026 flood. Users provide before-and-after, single-band GeoTIFFs prepared from matching NISAR GCOV data. The app displays both images and a color-coded radar-return difference preview, and flags pixels whose return decreased beyond a chosen threshold.

The prototype also has backend endpoints for searching the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) catalog for NISAR GCOV scenes and GOFF image pairs. However, users currently prepare and align the GeoTIFFs outside the app; it does not download or convert NISAR products.

Benefits and intended impact
Radar can collect observations day or night and through clouds, making it useful when optical imagery or field access is limited. The app aims to make radar comparisons easier for non-specialists to explore and discuss, and to help identify places where local reports, field checks, or validated datasets may be useful. Its intended impact is to support investigation and communication—not to make official flood, damage, or evacuation decisions.

Data and interpretation
The project focuses on NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar data distributed through ASF. Project materials describe a demonstration comparison using files labeled August 16 and September 12, 2026. A documented run reports 12.70 km² of candidate decrease pixels at the default −3 dB threshold. That is a screening result, not a confirmed flood extent: the event date falls between the observations, and radar-return changes can also result from soil moisture, vegetation, terrain, built surfaces, or imaging conditions. Source granule details should be verified before presenting the result as a scientific finding.

Tools, languages, and hardware
The backend is written in Python using FastAPI, Rasterio, and NumPy for API handling and raster analysis. The browser interface uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The project uses GeoTIFF inputs and ASF’s catalog API. GeoTIFF files have been created through OSGeo4W shell from HDF5 files. Development and use require a standard computer; no specialized hardware is needed. NISAR is the satellite mission supplying the radar observations.

What makes the project creative
The project turns a complex radar comparison into a simple “before, after, and what changed?” experience. It combines source-image previews with a color-coded difference view and a configurable threshold, while distinguishing candidate signal changes from confirmed real-world events. This makes the analysis more approachable without presenting uncertain results as fact.

Factors considered
The app checks that inputs have compatible dimensions, coordinate reference systems, and pixel grids, and requires projected data in metres to estimate area. Users must use the same band and polarization for both dates and select whether values are linear backscatter or already in decibels. The prototype also limits upload size and raster dimensions. The team considered uncertainty, event timing, accessibility for non-experts, and the risk of misinterpreting a radar change as proof of flooding.
